title: Fitness Technology
desc: Choose, set up and use wearables, apps and simple sensors to plan safe training and track progress honestly.
outcomes: Explain what common fitness sensors measure and where they are weak.
Set up a tracker and app for one training goal.
Read a week of data and spot patterns and errors.
Judge whether a device or app is accurate, private and worth its cost.
Build a 4-week safe training plan with a data log.
task: Build and follow a 4-week training plan for one willing adult or yourself, using one tracker and one app, with a weekly data review.
condition: A phone, one wearable or the phone sensors, a spreadsheet, two peers and a mentor. A qualified coach or doctor is asked first when health conditions exist.
standard: Plan is safe and written with a start check; data is logged on at least 24 of 28 days; at least two device errors are found and explained; privacy settings are reviewed; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Fitness instructors, gym staff, teachers, community sport leaders and anyone training with a device.
evidence: goal sheet, start check, device test notes, 28-day log, weekly reviews, privacy checklist
modules: Goals and a safe start
Understand
Technology helps only when the goal is clear and the start is safe.
Write one goal with a number and a date, such as walk 8,000 steps on five days a week for four weeks.
Do a start check: ask about illness, injury, medicines, pregnancy; if any apply, ask a doctor or qualified coach before you plan.
Never push through chest pain, dizziness or sharp pain; stop and seek help.
A learner wants to run 5 km. She notes a knee injury last year, asks a physiotherapist first, and chooses a walk-run plan for four weeks.
Write your goal and start check.
Set a goal with a number and date, and check any risk with a qualified person.
What sensors measure
Understand
Each sensor measures something indirectly, and every one has error.
Steps come from motion; heart rate from light on the skin or a chest strap; sleep from movement and heart rate; calories are estimates.
Light sensors can read less well on dark skin or over tattoos, and errors also grow with cold hands, loose straps and unusual movement.
Compare to a simple truth: count 100 steps by hand, or a 60-second pulse by finger.
A wrist band says 112 steps for a hand-counted 100: error 12%. Chest strap and band show 148 and 141 beats per minute in the same minute.
Test your device against two hand checks and record the error.
Calculate the error percentage, and write it next to each check.
Set up app, device and data
Apply
Good set-up avoids bad data.
Fit the device snugly; set height, weight and age correctly; choose the right activity type.
Sync daily; keep software updated; charge before sessions.
Decide what you will log: sessions, minutes, effort from 1 to 10, sleep hours, soreness.
A user finds steps double count while pushing a stroller; they turn that activity mode off and note it.
Set up and write a one-page set-up record.
Record the settings, pass the test sync, and give the log five fields.
Training plan basics
Create
A plan has progress, rest and variety.
Increase load slowly, about 10% a week; include two rest or light days.
Mix cardio, strength and mobility; warm up and cool down.
Write the plan as a week table with minutes, effort and the data to log.
Week 1: 3 walks of 30 minutes, 2 strength sessions of 20 minutes. Week 2: walks of 33 minutes.
Write a 4-week plan table.
Keep weekly increases to 10% or less, and schedule two rest days each week.
Reading the data
Analyse
Data is useful when you look at trends, not single days.
Use weekly averages; ignore one odd day.
Look for patterns: poor sleep before low effort days, high resting heart rate after illness.
Mark missing days and device errors; do not fill gaps with guesses.
The weekly average of resting heart rate rises from 62 to 68 after a cold; the plan eases for three days.
Review your first two weeks and write three findings.
Write findings that use averages, and name at least one data error.
Privacy, ethics and fairness
Evaluate
Health data is sensitive.
Read what the app collects and shares; turn off location sharing and public maps near your home.
Never share another person's data without clear consent; a coach or employer must not force data sharing.
Avoid comparing bodies in ways that shame; celebrate effort.
A school club shares only team totals and not names after pupils object.
Complete a privacy checklist for your app.
Review at least five settings, and write them down.
Choosing and costing a device
Evaluate
More expensive does not mean better.
List needs first: battery, water resistance, sensors, app support.
Compare 3 options on cost, battery days, accuracy tests, repair and resale; add the yearly cost of any subscription.
Prefer products with clear data export so you are not locked in.

Option B costs 6,000 INR (prices are estimates; check your market) with 10-day battery; option C costs 4,000 INR plus 1,200 INR a year. After two years of use, B is cheaper (6,000 INR against 6,400 INR for C).
Build a comparison table for 3 devices with the currency written.
Calculate the totals over two years correctly.
Review, share and sustain
Create
Finish the 4 weeks and plan the next.
Compare results to the goal; write what worked and what to change.
Present to your peer circle; invite one improvement.
Plan device reuse or recycling at end of life.
Goal met on 4 of 5 weeks; sleep log shows late phone use; next plan adds a screen-off time at 10 pm.
Present your results.
Use real data in the results, and plan one change.
quiz: Name two sensor errors.
A loose strap; dark skin or a tattoo (for light sensors); steps counted twice.
Why ask a doctor first for some people?
Illness, injury or medicines can make some exercise unsafe.
How can you test a step counter?
Count 100 steps by hand and compare.
What weekly increase is a common safe guide?
About 10%.
Why use weekly averages?
They hide single-day noise and show trends.
Name two privacy settings.
Location sharing and public activity maps.
What is subscription lock-in?
You lose data or features when you stop paying.
How do you treat missing days?
Mark them; do not invent numbers.
Why include rest days?
The body adapts and recovers during rest.
What do you do on sharp pain?
Stop and seek qualified help.
rubric: Safe plan with progress and rest explained
Plan results reported without the tracker data
Weekly tracker figures match the log, with gaps stated
Weekly figures match the log and each change to the plan cites the week it came from
Readiness screen done, consent written, stop rules listed
Screen, consent and stop rules checked by a qualified person, with a doctor-referral line
jobs: Sets up devices and apps for members
Uses data to guide safe training
next: wearable sensor basics, nutrition awareness, data literacy.
local: Rules on health data differ by place. Use only consented data and keep it private.
